title: The Brahmanas Repent
story:
The sacrifice had everything a sacrifice should have: the right place, the right hour, the right offerings, the right mantras, and fires tended by priests who knew every rule. The brahmanas had given themselves to it completely — so completely, the verses say, that when a young cowherd came to them asking for food, sent by his companion Krishna, who waited hungry in the forest with his friends, they had waved him away. There were rules to follow. There was no time for a cowherd's errand.

It was their wives who had gone instead, carrying food through the woods to Krishna and his friends while their husbands stayed behind with the fire. Now the women came home, and the brahmanas looked at them, and something in their faces stopped the men where they stood. Even the one wife whose husband had held her back by force had not been stopped; she had simply closed her eyes and gone to Krishna in her mind, meditating on the Lord exactly as she had heard of him. And Krishna, for his part, had fed the cowherds with the very food the women had carried through the woods.

Then the full knowledge of it reached them, the way a slow truth reaches a man who has been busy elsewhere. The one they had refused was Vishnu himself — the Lord, standing in the forest in the shape of a cowherd boy, and they had turned him away for the sake of a ritual. The verses record what they said to one another, and it is not a proud speech. "Shame on our birth," they said, "and on its threefold aims. Shame on our vows. Shame on our great learning." For the Lord's power to delude, they understood, could bewilder even the wise, even the yogis. And look — look at these women. They had no initiation into the brahminical way, no long years of study in a guru's house, and yet they loved Krishna, the teacher of all the worlds, with a love so complete it shamed everything the men had spent their lives acquiring.

So the brahmanas spoke of what they now saw. The place of the sacrifice, the hour, the separate offerings, the mantras, the priests, the fires — these were not separate things, not tools to be arranged. They were all Krishna himself. He it was whom the goddess of fortune serves, turning away from all others, ever longing for the touch of his feet. He it was who needs nothing and yet grants liberation to those who ask. "Salutations to the Lord Krishna," they said, "whose wisdom never falters. He is Vishnu himself, the lord of all lords of yoga, the first being of all — and it is his own power that keeps our minds deluded." They remembered their own fault, the insult they had offered him, and they wanted, more than anything, to look upon him.

But they did not go. They did not dare. Kamsa ruled nearby, and they were afraid. So the men who knew every verse of the ritual sat at home and longed for the boy they had turned away, praising him in words they had never once thought to speak beside the fire.
reflection: The brahmanas' lament is really a confession that their ritual had become an end in itself — something performed without remembering whom it was for. The women, who knew none of the rules, had found the one the rules point to.
hero_scene: The brahmanas gathered in their home at night, their sacrificial fire burning low, as they sit bowed with their heads in their hands, faces lifted with regret toward the doorway through which their wives have just returned, their devotion to Krishna hanging unspoken in the air.
